papers.title: WebCoder: Scaling General Frontend Development with Artifact-Grounded Agentic Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Real-world frontend development requires agents to compose reproduction, generation, modification, and repair over an evolving application state. Learning a general policy for this process requires translating heterogeneous execution feedback into task-aligned rewards and effective credit assignment across long sequences of interdependent actions. We introduce WebCoder, a general frontend development agent trained with artifact-grounded agentic reinforcement learning. Our key idea is to assess diverse development activities through their effects on a shared executable artifact and its satisfaction of task requirements. We build Webdev-World, an executable environment that integrates code editing, application execution, browser inspection, and on-demand skills while preserving project state across interactions. An independent verifier evaluates the final application against task requirements to provide terminal rewards, while changes in intermediate artifact progress redistribute the resulting rollout advantage across development segments. Context compaction and message-tree sample construction support training on trajectories beyond a single context window while avoiding repeated loss computation on shared generated history. We further introduce Webdev-Bench to evaluate composed development requirements within a single project. On Webdev-Bench, WebCoder-27B raises requirement satisfaction from 64.8 for its Qwen3.8-27B base model to 72.8, exceeding Claude-Opus-4.8 (65.1) and GPT-5.4 (59.6); on Vision2Web, it improves the average visual and functional score from 41.1 to 62.4, on par with Claude-Opus-4.8. Ablation studies confirm the contributions of artifact-grounded credit assignment and long-horizon training.

papers.title: MS-Eval: Benchmarking Sub-Agent Delegation and Orchestration in MCP-Intensive Working Scenarios
papers.abstract: LLM agents are increasingly integrated into real-world works, yet they must handle diverse domain-specific tools and complex multi-sub-task problems that sequential tool invocation resolves inefficiently and with severe context bloat. The Main-Agent Delegation and Sub-Agent Execution (MAD-SAE) paradigm addresses these issues by delegating sub-tasks to specialized sub-agents for parallel execution in isolated contexts, but its delegation and orchestration quality remains unquantified. We introduce MS-Eval, a unified evaluation kit comprising an MCP-intensive benchmark, a controlled execution harness, tailored delegation and orchestration metrics, and the MSQ index for comprehensive assessment. Evaluating four MAD-SAE variants and eight frontier models reveals that (1) sub-agent specialization (Spec) is the best practical practice; (2) open-source models are largely competitive with few exceptions; and (3) MAD-SAE generally raises cost with contingent payoff, benefiting most open-source models in both performance and efficiency while leaving closed-source models with higher cost and degraded performance. Our case study further traces these gains to better single-agent solutions, effective context offloading, and genuine sub-task parallelism, whereas unnecessary or redundant delegation turns the same cost into pure overhead. Codes: this https URL

papers.title: FuTransformer: FP8 prefill and INT4 decode for Llama-style inference on Hopper
papers.abstract: Transformer prefill reuses weights across tokens and is dominated by matrix multiplication and activation data movement; single-token decode has limited reuse and is dominated by weight and KV-cache reads. We present FUTRANSFORMER, a CUDA implementation of a Llama-style Transformer block for NVIDIA Hopper GPUs. It applies CODA's GEMM-plus-epilogue approach to inference, adding direct KV-cache placement, folding the fixed RMSNorm gain into weights, writing FP8 output directly with delayed scaling, and supporting prefill without padding. Decode uses INT4 projection weights and an INT4 KV-cache copy. Weights and keys follow Tensor Core fragment layouts for direct dequantization into MMA operands without full intermediate tiles. A block-diagonal Hadamard transform reduces cache quantization error from outlier channels. On one H100, prefill is up to 1.48x faster than compiled PyTorch FP8 and reaches 1.29 PFLOP/s. For gate/up projection with SwiGLU at the 8B shape, our BF16 path is 1.13x faster than CODA. Our FP8 path is 2.02-2.18x faster than the evaluated BF16 CODA path. Across 8B and 70B shapes at batches 1-32, INT4 decode is 1.3-2.4x faster than the faster of PyTorch's BF16 and INT4 blocks at each point: 2.1-3.3x faster than compiled, CUDA-graphed BF16 and 1.3-6.3x faster than the same block using PyTorch's INT4 projection kernel, which targets a single query row and loses to BF16 at batch 32. It is also 31-51% faster than our FP8 path. Complete Llama-3.1-8B decode takes 2.8 ms per step at batch one, versus 8.1 ms for the compiled transformers implementation. Decoding every WikiText-2 token through the INT4 weight path raises perplexity from 6.24 to 7.23 with round-to-nearest weights or 6.99 with GPTQ in the same format; the rotated INT4 cache adds 0.20. The kernels match a quantized reference computation within 0.001 perplexity.

papers.title: RL-Guided Temporal Localization for Dual-Channel Retrieval in Long-Horizon Agent Memory
papers.abstract: Time-aware retrieval is crucial for long-horizon LLM agents to effectively leverage ever-growing long-term memory. Existing methods focus on lexical or semantic similarity, leading to target memories being crowded out by temporally mismatched yet semantically similar candidates. Even time-aware approaches inject temporal cues only during memory organization or answer generation, overlooking temporal constraints at the retrieval stage, where candidate selection occurs - the root cause of the displacement. Inspired by the temporal contiguity effect in human episodic memory, we propose TIDER (Temporal Interval-driven Dual-channel Evidence Retrieval), a time-aware agentic retrieval framework. Central to TIDER is a reinforcement learning (RL)-trained temporal interval locator that infers the temporal windows in which the evidence lies. RL optimizes window localization as a discrete, non-differentiable retrieval decision, using composite rewards to convert sparse answer supervision into fine-grained retrieval feedback. These temporal windows first define the temporal retrieval channel; the retrieved candidates are then merged with results from the semantic channel and reranked by proximity to the windows. This temporal grounding enables TIDER to retrieve temporally aligned evidence that would otherwise be drowned out by the volume of semantically similar yet temporally mismatched memories. With a lightweight 1.7B locator, TIDER achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on both long-horizon memory benchmarks - 61.52% on LifeBench (+8.82%) and 78.96% on LoCoMo (+3.66%) - which indicates that temporal cues are crucial for pinpointing target evidence amid a vast pool of semantically similar historical events in long-term daily-life memory.

papers.title: Agentic In-Context Learning: What Algorithms Can Transformers Learn in Closed-Loop Interaction?
papers.abstract: The learning algorithm view of in-context learning (ICL) studies how fixed-parameter Transformers learn from supplied examples. Language model agents extend this setting through interaction: their actions determine what evidence enters context next. We call this regime Agentic In-Context Learning (Agentic ICL). Existing studies largely depend on externally supplied contexts or reward-bearing interaction histories, while work on general tool-using agents lacks a learning algorithm view. We represent an interactive learner by its state, update, and decision rule, covering active learning, bandits, and online reinforcement learning (RL). For expressivity, we construct causal Transformers that approximate these algorithms over a finite horizon, and bound the resulting loss in return. For training, we characterize when optimizing process rewards preserves behavior that maximizes the final outcome. Distillation experiments show that Transformers can learn to execute three representative recursions. We then train models from outcome or process rewards without oracle action or state targets, as in RL post-training. Different rewards yield distinct decision policies. Improving the alignment of process supervision with outcome-optimal action preferences shifts learned decisions accordingly. Such behavioral differences persist in a pretrained language model across textual paraphrases.

papers.title: From Approval to Abuse: Privilege Escalation Attacks on Harness-Protected Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Coding agents use execution harnesses to constrain the consequences of prompt injection by enforcing permission boundaries. These systems deterministically intercept any out-of-sandbox action and prompt the user for approval. To reduce approval fatigue, users can approve allow-rules proposed by the agent, after which any future action matching the rule is allowed without a prompt. In this work, we show that this mechanism introduces a new risk: untrusted context can influence the permissions presented for approval, with consequences extending beyond the immediate task. We investigate privilege escalation targeting this permission-update process. Specifically, adversarial context planted in a repository can reliably steer an agent performing a routine task into requesting a plausibly justified, yet dangerously broad allow-rule. If the user approves the request, the saved rule can effectively blind the harness, enabling adversaries to execute malicious actions that would otherwise require approval, without triggering human oversight. Across production platforms, including Claude Code and Codex CLI, we demonstrate that agents successfully elicit the target allow-rules in 58% of experimental instances. Once acquired, these rules exhibit a massive semantic blast radius, covering 56.9% of category-specific capability test cases. To further quantify the downstream risk, we show that conditional on rule approval, our exploit achieves verified, silent goal completion in 47 of the 58 eligible instances (81.0%), undermining the safety promise of human-in-the-loop oversight.

papers.title: From Relevant Memories to Sufficient Evidence: Rethinking Memory Utilization in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Long-term memory enables LLM agents to reuse past experiences, yet retrieving relevant memories does not necessarily provide sufficient evidence for answering a query. Essential information may remain fragmented across memory records, obscured by abstraction, or disconnected from the relations required for reasoning. We identify this relevance-sufficiency gap and propose QEMem, a framework that reformulates memory utilization as the construction of query-specific evidence sets, shifting the focus from individual retrieval relevance to collective evidential support. QEMem integrates three complementary mechanisms: query-guided discovery retrieves evidence across multiple memory granularities; source-grounded reification organizes it into structured ViewCards with explicit evidential roles and source references; and sufficiency-guided refinement selectively recovers missing information. Operating on existing memory stores without modifying memory formation, QEMem achieves 91.43% LLM-judge accuracy on LoCoMo with Claude Opus 4.5, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline, MemR$^3$, by 7.6 percentage points and NEMORI by 10.7 points under a shared memory store. Further analyses demonstrate improved evidence coverage and strong performance on questions requiring cross-session evidence integration.

papers.title: Doc2Harness: Benchmarking LLMs on Long-Horizon Harness Engineering of Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Agents driven by large language models are increasingly deployed on long-horizon tasks, where they use tools and modify real workspaces. How well they perform depends as much on the harness around the model as on the model itself. Existing benchmarks measure downstream task success under a fixed harness, leaving harness engineering itself unexplored. We propose Doc2Harness, a two-stage benchmark that evaluates long-horizon harness engineering directly. In Stage 1, a build model operating inside a fixed builder harness receives an interface-only contract skeleton and a development document that consolidates behavior across twelve frontier harnesses, and then constructs a complete candidate harness in an isolated container. In Stage 2, the frozen candidate harness runs in containers separate from the construction environment, one per test case, and is driven end to end by a scripted mock model. We score each test case using four observable channels, namely the requests sent to the model, the files on disk, the process exit code, and the command output; positive controls rule out vacuous passes. Across nineteen frontier models, each evaluated with three independent builds on 328 test cases, GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest pass rate at 53.05%, while the weakest model reaches 27.44%, a gap of roughly twenty-six percentage points. Even the strongest model fails nearly half of the test cases, and failures cluster around how cross-cutting functionality is split across modules. To our knowledge, Doc2Harness provides the first deterministic benchmark for measuring long-horizon harness engineering.

papers.title: Enforcing Code Reasoning in Agentic Scaffold for More Effective Issue Resolution
papers.abstract: Reasoning is central to ReAct-based programming agents, yet whether and how they reason about code remains unclear. We study 7,955 issue-resolution trajectories from six single- and multi-agent scaffolds across four programming languages on SWE-bench-Verified, SWE-bench-Pro, and SWE-bench-Lite. We identify 12 forms of code reasoning in 66.95% of trajectories. Code reasoning is associated with higher resolution rates, and its intensity increases with task complexity. However, it remains largely unguided: agents may focus on surface-level symptoms during localization, fail to refine near-correct patches, overlook issue requirements, and generate tests with limited behavioral diversity. To address these limitations, we propose DeskCheck, an agentic scaffold that systematically guides code reasoning throughout repository-level issue resolution. DeskCheck simulates execution paths to localize root causes, simulates candidate patches to refine near-misses, audits patches against issue requirements, and reasons about corner-case inputs and expected outputs before generating tests. On 731 SWE-bench-Pro instances, DeskCheck improves resolution rates over mini-SWE-Agent and Claude Code by 6.29% to 10.53%, at an additional cost of $0.02-$0.28 per instance (average: $0.14). Per-phase analyses show higher method-level localization recall, more successful repairs of imprecisely localized issues, and better detection of missed corner cases in near-correct patches. Exact McNemar tests show statistically significant improvements across all subject LLMs (p < 10^-10), while repeated experiments support robustness to agent nondeterminism. These findings motivate systematic code reasoning as a means of improving programming agents.

papers.title: AuditKIT: A Unified Evaluation Spine for Benchmarking, Judging, and Comparing Large Language Models and Agentic Systems
papers.abstract: Evaluating language models and agents requires combining benchmark accuracy, judge-based assessment, runtime performance, tool-use behavior, and retrieval quality. Differences in interfaces, metric semantics, and trace formats complicate these comparisons and can hide failures in agentic workflows. We present AuditKIT, a source-available evaluation library that records these measurements in one result representation, with direction-aware metric contracts, configuration fingerprints, and extensible metrics and backends. For agents, it provides turn-aware tool-call matching, separates parallel from sequential execution, and distinguishes verified task outcomes from trajectory-level diagnostics. Missing or unobservable evidence is marked unscored rather than counted as failure. For retrieval-augmented generation, it combines ranked retrieval metrics, judged grounding, and deterministic evidence checks. Seven case studies spanning model comparison, serving runtimes, retrieval, tool calling, and interoperability show how answer extraction, runtime behavior, and metric selection change evaluation outcomes.

papers.title: Towards Agentic Proof Harness Engineering
papers.abstract: Formal verification of real-world projects requires substantial manual effort, from specifying correctness properties to constructing the infrastructure needed to check them. We envision verification agents that assist developers throughout this process. Among the many tasks involved, one stands out as both foundational and amenable to automation: proof-harness engineering. A proof harness defines an isolated verification environment for a program unit, such as a function or module, by providing symbolic inputs, initialization code, and models of its dependencies. Today, proof-harness engineering remains largely a manual task performed by verification engineers. To explore the potential of coding agents for this task, we propose an agentic proof-harness engineer that automatically constructs verifier-ready harnesses from a software project and a designated verification target. We combine the agent with formal soundness and precision guards to validate generated abstractions and guide their refinement. We evaluate the feasibility of our approach in an exploratory case study on curl and libuv, using three historical assertion violations already embedded in the source code as verification properties. Our results show that the agent successfully constructs proof harnesses that enable CBMC to detect all three violations. We further demonstrate the potential for reusing these harnesses with other verification tools.

topic.title: Designing for Imperfect Prompts: A Simulation-Based Evaluation of an LLM-Based Enterprise Data Assistant Using Knowledge Graphs
topic.abstract: Enterprise data assistants using large language models (LLMs) promise democratized data access in organizations. Yet in our real-world deployment within the CFO unit's data lake at an industry partner, we observed that business users frequently pose imperfect prompts that include domain-specific vocabulary and lack schema references or structural information. This Design Science Research study examines automatic resolution using a semantic mediation layer. We design and evaluate two design variants: schema-based mediation via semantic similarity, and knowledge graph-based mediation leveraging an automatically constructed knowledge graph from the data lake. Our simulation-based evaluation using real-world data, supported by LLM-as-a-Judge assessments and human validation, shows that knowledge graph-based mediation outperforms the schema-based approach in Precision, Recall, F1, and preserving user intent. We propose a design principle for knowledge graph-based mediation, demonstrating that structured knowledge representation bridges user intent and database structure and guides the design of enterprise data assistants across skill levels.

topic.title: An Error Taxonomy for Property Graph Data
topic.abstract: Graph data are increasingly used in applications where relationships and topology matter. Yet, compared to tabular data, the notions of data quality and error types for graphs are less established. Tabular error concepts often fail to capture structural properties and context inherent in graph data, hindering systematic quality assessment in graph-based systems. We focus on property graphs (PGs) in graph databases. PGs are often managed without a prescriptive schema, enabling data insertion without explicit validation, while still exhibiting an implicit schema of recurring structural patterns. Irregularities in these patterns may indicate errors, but their interpretation depends on the surrounding graph context. To address these challenges, we provide a systematic view of errors in graph data by proposing a comprehensive graph-specific taxonomy of error types. To position these errors with respect to established work on tabular data quality, we derive a mapping between graph errors and corresponding error notions in tabular data. This mapping highlights which concepts transfer across data models and where structural properties of graphs introduce fundamentally different challenges requiring extensions. Overall, the taxonomy and mapping provide a shared vocabulary for describing, characterizing, comparing, and studying graph data errors, and they lay the groundwork for future work on error detection and repair in graph data.

topic.title: An Interactive GraphRAG Workspace for Reifying, Auditing, and Steering Conversational AI Memories
topic.abstract: Conversational Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely employed in software engineering for code generation, debugging, and architectural design. However, as developers engage in multi-session development tasks, technical knowledge becomes siloed in isolated, linear chat histories. Reusing context across sessions leads to three critical challenges: (1) flat-vector retrieval fails to traverse multi-hop relational dependencies between distant architectural decisions; (2) temporal drift in software packages and APIs results in silent context poisoning when reusing aged dialogue logs; and (3) raw conversation concatenation induces prompt bloat and attention degradation. We present CognitiveCanvas, an interactive tool that transforms conversational AI memories from ephemeral text logs into persistent, manipulable, and audited knowledge objects. \textsc{CognitiveCanvas} integrates: (1) a Hierarchical Semantic Fact-Graph (HSFG) that distills dialogues into Goal, Fact, and Code artifacts, achieving a 92.2\% token reduction while enabling multi-hop GraphRAG traversal; (2) a Continuous Temporal Drift Auditor coupling 60+ regex heuristics with live calendar-anchored LLM verification for 1-click self-correction; and (3) a Spatial-Symbolic Prompt Compiler (SSPC) that translates 2D direct manipulation gestures (Voronoi clustering, node resizing, synthesis edges) directly into structured attention directives

topic.title: AgentOnto: Ontology-Guided LLM Agents for Enterprise Data Analytics
topic.abstract: Enterprise data analysis requires agents to connect analytical requests with knowledge distributed across databases, business documents, and existing example tasks. Without an explicit representation of this knowledge, an agent may produce incorrect analytical results and cannot reliably incorporate feedback. We present AgentOnto, an ontology-guided LLM agent for enterprise data analytics. AgentOnto organizes heterogeneous enterprise knowledge into an ontology that directly guides analysis and incorporates confirmed feedback. Iterative Ontology Preparation further improves the ontology through self-generated analysis tasks. We evaluate AgentOnto on two public data sources. AgentOnto substantially outperforms representative methods, while module-level evaluations confirm the effectiveness of ontology construction, analysis, and updating. A real-world deployment further demonstrates its practical value in enterprise analytics. These results demonstrate that explicitly constructing, using, and updating enterprise knowledge supports reliable and adaptable data analysis.

topic.title: Logic-Guided Graph Denoising Diffusion Models
topic.abstract: Graph diffusion models are competitive approaches for generating complex graph-structured data. However, when such distributions have strict structural constraints, diffusion models may fail to capture them exactly, resulting in the generation of invalid graphs. In this paper, we propose a method for grounding graph diffusion models in domain-specific knowledge via First Order Logic (FOL), leveraging its expressive and interpretable formalism to impose structural constraints on the generative process. We incorporate domain knowledge using classifier guidance, a technique that conditions the diffusion model's distribution on external variables to exert control over the sampled data. During the generative process, classifier guidance steers the denoising trajectory to optimize an objective function, which we define as a fuzzy and differentiable relaxation of the logical rules. Our methodology requires only the specification of constraints in FOL, whose satisfaction is encouraged at inference time to guide a pre-trained generative model. We evaluate our approach by comparing the unconditional generation of knowledge graphs with our logic-guided framework, which incorporates domain ontologies as structural constraints during inference. This approach significantly increases the proportion of generated graphs that satisfy the ontological constraints.
